trial.title: Frequency-Dependent Effects of Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation on Autonomic and Cardiovascular Parameters

endpoints.measure: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) Changes (ΔRMSSD, ΔHF, ΔLF/HF)
endpoints.time_frame: Pre- vs Post-stimulation (5-min segments)(5-minute baseline, 5-minute stimulation, 5-minute post period)
endpoints.description:
HRV is recorded using a validated high-resolution heart rate monitor (Polar H10) during a 5-minute resting baseline (T0) and a 5-minute post-stimulation period (T2).

The following time- and frequency-domain parameters are analyzed: RMSSD, HF (ms²), and LF/HF ratio.

Artefact correction is performed using standard HRV processing methods. Acute autonomic response is quantified by calculating change scores (Δ = post-pre) for each stimulation frequency.

endpoints.time_frame: Pre- vs Post-stimulation (5-minute baseline, 5-minute stimulation, 5-minute post period)
endpoints.description:
Two readings are taken at each time point from the right arm with a validated automatic sphygmomanometer, and the average systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressure values are used for analysis.

Changes are calculated as post-pre (Δ values) to assess the acute physiological effect of each stimulation frequency..

endpoints.time_frame: Pre- vs Post-stimulation (5-minute video segments) (5-minute baseline, 5-minute stimulation, 5-minute post period)
endpoints.description:
Respiratory rate is assessed by video-based thoracoabdominal motion tracking at baseline (T0) and after stimulation (T2).

Videos are analyzed using Kinovea motion-tracking software, and a 1-minute stable segment is used to determine breaths per minute by counting inspiratory peaks.

Respiratory changes are expressed as Δ values (post-pre) to account for individual differences and improve HRV interpretability.Respiratory rate is assessed by video-based thoracoabdominal motion tracking at baseline (T0) and after stimulation (T2).

endpoints.time_frame: Pre- vs Post-stimulation (5-minute baseline, 5-minute stimulation, 5-minute post period)
endpoints.description:
Participants report their perceived discomfort level at baseline (T0) and immediately after stimulation (T2) using a 0-10 Visual Analog Scale (VAS).

The scale captures any sensory discomfort associated with tcVNS. Changes are calculated by subtracting the pre-stimulation score from the post-stimulation score (ΔVAS).

analysis_trace: Trial NCT07274332 is a randomized, sham-controlled, crossover study investigating frequency-dependent effects of transcutaneous cervical vagus nerve stimulation (tcVNS) at 0 Hz (sham), 10 Hz, 25 Hz, 50 Hz, and 100 Hz in healthy adults (18-30 years). Primary endpoint: HRV changes (ΔRMSSD, ΔHF, ΔLF/HF). Secondary endpoints: Blood Pressure (SBP, DBP, MAP), Respiratory Rate, and Discomfort Level (VAS 0-10).

Evidence retrieved: (1) PMC11940630 - taVNS frequency/pulse width study showing 10Hz/250μs and 25Hz/100μs increased SDNN but not RMSSD; (2) PMC9508455 - taVNS showed LF/HF ratio changes; (3) PMC9632923 - taVNS 25Hz improved morning HRV with vagal activity increases; (4) PMC12061502 - taVNS 100Hz reduced HR with minimal BP changes during exercise; (5) PMC10114770 - tcVNS lengthened exhalation time vs sham.

Evidence-role assessment: Direct numeric evidence for cervical tcVNS at exact frequencies is limited. Auricular (taVNS) studies provide indirect directional evidence for HRV effects. Cervical-specific evidence (PMC10114770) supports respiratory effects. No direct evidence for 10/25/50/100 Hz dose-response in cervical tcVNS.

Primary-0 (HRV): Based on taVNS literature, low-frequency stimulation (10-25 Hz) shows modest HRV effects. RMSSD and HF (vagal markers) may increase slightly at lower frequencies (10-25 Hz). LF/HF ratio expected to decrease with effective vagal activation. Higher frequencies (50-100 Hz) show less consistent HRV effects. Crossover design with n=36 provides adequate power.

Secondary-0 (BP): Literature shows minimal acute BP effects in healthy volunteers. Yoshida 2025 (taVNS 100Hz) showed minimal BP change during exercise. tcVNS may reduce SBP slightly (~2-5 mmHg) but effects are small and variable in normotensive healthy adults.

Secondary-1 (Respiratory Rate): PMC10114770 demonstrated tcVNS lengthens exhalation time, suggesting reduced respiratory rate. Effect likely small (1-2 breaths/min decrease) with dose-response favoring lower frequencies.
Secondary-2 (Discomfort): tcVNS at sensory threshold is generally well-tolerated. VAS increase expected to be mild (<2 points) with potential frequency-dependent increase at 100Hz.

Key uncertainties: (1) Cervical vs auricular anatomical differences; (2) Exact frequency-response curve for cervical tcVNS; (3) 10-minute stimulation duration may limit effect magnitude; (4) Sham control adequacy with 0 Hz.

Success probability: High likelihood of detecting frequency-dependent HRV effects (primary endpoint) given crossover design and validated measures. Study is basic science with physiological endpoints, not clinical efficacy trial.
